Complex Numbers

Purdue University
Course-material provenance

This page was migrated from the CHM 696 course materials developed by Jonathan Hood and Lyudmila Slipchenko. Equations and examples remain under editorial review during the Fall 2026 website migration.

Learning goals¶

After this lecture, you should be able to:

  • move between Cartesian and polar forms of a complex number;

  • perform arithmetic, powers, and roots in the most convenient form;

  • use Euler’s formula to derive trigonometric and hyperbolic identities;

  • distinguish the multivalued complex logarithm from its principal branch; and

  • interpret complex amplitudes in physical applications.

Definition and notation¶

A complex number has Cartesian form

z=x+iy,x,y∈R,z=x+\mathrm{i}y,\qquad x,y\in\mathbb{R},z=x+iy,x,y∈R,
(1)

with

Re⁡z=x,Im⁡z=y.\operatorname{Re}z=x,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=y.Rez=x,Imz=y.
(2)

It can also be identified with the ordered pair (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) or written in polar form:

z=r(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)=reiθ,r=∣z∣=x2+y2.z=r(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)=r e^{\mathrm{i}\theta}, \qquad r=|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.z=r(cosθ+isinθ)=reiθ,r=∣z∣=x2+y2​.
(3)

The angle θ\thetaθ is an argument (or phase) of zzz. Arguments that differ by 2πk2\pi k2πk, k∈Zk\in\mathbb{Z}k∈Z, describe the same nonzero complex number.

What the original figure plots. It plots one point zzz in the complex plane. The horizontal coordinate is x=Re⁡zx=\operatorname{Re}zx=Rez, the vertical coordinate is y=Im⁡zy=\operatorname{Im}zy=Imz, the arrow from the origin has length rrr, and the angle from the real axis is θ\thetaθ. The handwritten equations show three descriptions of that same point: (x,y)(x,y)(x,y), x+iyx+\mathrm{i}yx+iy, and r(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)r(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)r(cosθ+isinθ).

What this is trying to convey. A complex number is one point described in two coordinate systems. The horizontal and vertical projections give xxx and yyy; the same geometry gives the modulus rrr and argument θ\thetaθ.

What the original figure plots. It plots z=x+iyz=x+\mathrm{i}yz=x+iy above the real axis and its conjugate zˉ=x−iy\bar z=x-\mathrm{i}yzˉ=x−iy below it. Both arrows have length rrr and the same horizontal coordinate xxx; their vertical coordinates are yyy and −y-y−y, and their angles are ϕ\phiϕ and −ϕ-\phi−ϕ.

What this is trying to convey. Complex conjugation changes only the sign of the imaginary component. Geometrically, that is a reflection across the real axis: the real part and modulus stay fixed while the argument changes sign.

Warning

Use radians in analytical formulas involving derivatives, series, or integrals. Degrees may be used for numerical angle calculations only after the relevant formulas have been interpreted consistently.

Complex conjugate¶

  • A complex number: z=x+iyz = x + \mathrm{i}yz=x+iy

  • Complex conjugate: zˉ=z∗=x−iy\bar{z} = z^* = x - \mathrm{i}yzˉ=z∗=x−iy

  • zˉ=r(cos⁡(−θ)+isin⁡(−θ))=r(cos⁡(θ)−isin⁡(θ))=re−iθ\bar{z} = r(\cos(-\theta) + i \sin(-\theta)) = r(\cos(\theta) - i \sin(\theta)) = re^{-i\theta}zˉ=r(cos(−θ)+isin(−θ))=r(cos(θ)−isin(θ))=re−iθ

What the original figure plots. This is the same reflection for the specific pair 2+3i2+3\mathrm{i}2+3i and 2−3i2-3\mathrm{i}2−3i. The two arrows end at (2,3)(2,3)(2,3) and (2,−3)(2,-3)(2,−3) and make angles θ\thetaθ and −θ-\theta−θ with the real axis.

What this is trying to convey. The abstract reflection rule should also be checkable in a concrete example. The pair 2+3i2+3\mathrm{i}2+3i and 2−3i2-3\mathrm{i}2−3i has the same real coordinate and magnitude, but opposite imaginary coordinates and arguments.

Complex Algebra: Addition, Multiplication, Division¶

(x1+iy1)+(x2+iy2)=(x1+x2)+i(y1+y2),(x1+iy1)(x2+iy2)=(x1x2−y1y2)+i(x1y2+y1x2).\begin{aligned} (x_1+\mathrm{i}y_1)+(x_2+\mathrm{i}y_2) &= (x_1+x_2)+\mathrm{i}(y_1+y_2),\\ (x_1+\mathrm{i}y_1)(x_2+\mathrm{i}y_2) &= (x_1x_2-y_1y_2)+\mathrm{i}(x_1y_2+y_1x_2). \end{aligned}(x1​+iy1​)+(x2​+iy2​)(x1​+iy1​)(x2​+iy2​)​=(x1​+x2​)+i(y1​+y2​),=(x1​x2​−y1​y2​)+i(x1​y2​+y1​x2​).​
(4)

Complex Series¶

  • Convergence of series involving complex numbers is defined analogously to that of real numbers, i.e., the series is convergent if its partial sum Sn=Xn+iYnS_n =X_n + \mathrm{i}Y_nSn​=Xn​+iYn​ approaches a limit S=X+iYS =X + \mathrm{i}YS=X+iY as n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞.

  • Practically, it means that Xn→XX_n \to XXn​→X and Yn→YY_n \to YYn​→Y.

  • For complex-numbered series, an absolutely convergent series converges. Therefore, we can test the absolute convergence.

  • In the complex power series ∑anzn\sum a_n z^n∑an​zn, where zzz and ana_nan​ are complex numbers, we are interested in a disk of convergence, with its radius called the radius of convergence.

Note

Example Find the disk of convergence for

1−z+z22−z33+⋯=1+∑n=1∞(−1)nznn.1-z+\frac{z^2}{2}-\frac{z^3}{3}+\cdots =1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n z^n}{n}.1−z+2z2​−3z3​+⋯=1+n=1∑∞​n(−1)nzn​.
(5)
Note

Example Find the disk of convergence for ∑n=0∞(z+1−i)n3nn2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(z+1-i)^n}{3^n n^2}∑n=0∞​3nn2(z+1−i)n​

Euler’s formula and polar form¶

Euler’s formula is

eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ.e^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta.eiθ=cosθ+isinθ.
(6)

  • Recall from the last lecture:

sin⁡θ=θ−θ3/3!+θ5/5!−⋯\sin\theta = \theta - \theta^3/3! + \theta^5/5! - \cdotssinθ=θ−θ3/3!+θ5/5!−⋯
(7)
cos⁡θ=1−θ2/2!+θ4/4!+⋯\cos\theta = 1 - \theta^2/2! + \theta^4/4! + \cdotscosθ=1−θ2/2!+θ4/4!+⋯
(8)

  • Now write the series for eiθe^{\mathrm{i}\theta}eiθ for real θ\thetaθ:

eiθ=1+iθ+(iθ)22!+(iθ)33!+(iθ)44!+(iθ)55!+⋯=1+iθ−θ22!−iθ33!+θ44!+iθ55!+⋯=1−θ22!+θ44!+⋯+i(θ−θ33!+θ55!+⋯ )=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ\begin{aligned} e^{\mathrm{i}\theta} &= 1 + \mathrm{i}\theta + \frac{(\mathrm{i}\theta)^2}{2!} + \frac{(\mathrm{i}\theta)^3}{3!} + \frac{(\mathrm{i}\theta)^4}{4!} + \frac{(\mathrm{i}\theta)^5}{5!} + \cdots \\ = 1 + \mathrm{i}\theta - \frac{\theta^2}{2!} -\mathrm{i}\frac{\theta^3}{3!} + \frac{\theta^4}{4!} + \mathrm{i}\frac{\theta^5}{5!} + \cdots \\ = 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2!} + \frac{\theta^4}{4!} + \cdots + \mathrm{i}\left (\theta - \frac{\theta^3}{3!} + \frac{\theta^5}{5!} + \cdots \right ) \\ &= \cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta \end{aligned}eiθ=1+iθ−2!θ2​−i3!θ3​+4!θ4​+i5!θ5​+⋯=1−2!θ2​+4!θ4​+⋯+i(θ−3!θ3​+5!θ5​+⋯)​=1+iθ+2!(iθ)2​+3!(iθ)3​+4!(iθ)4​+5!(iθ)5​+⋯=cosθ+isinθ​
(9)

  • We arrived to the polar form of a complex number: z=reiθz=re^{\mathrm{i}\theta}z=reiθ.

Cartesian to polar and back¶

Note

Example Convert z=−1+3 iz=-1+\sqrt{3}\,\mathrm{i}z=−1+3​i to polar form reiθre^{\mathrm{i}\theta}reiθ.

Note

Example Convert 2e−iπ/22e^{-\mathrm{i}\pi /2}2e−iπ/2 to Cartesian form.

What the original figure plots. It plots the point eiθe^{\mathrm{i}\theta}eiθ on a circle of radius one. The horizontal projection of the point is cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ and its vertical projection is sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ.

What this is trying to convey. On the unit circle the modulus is one, so a complex exponential is determined entirely by its angle. Its horizontal and vertical projections are exactly cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ and sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ.

The ordinary arctangent does not by itself determine the quadrant of a complex number. Numerically, use a two-argument function such as θ=atan2⁡(y,x)\theta=\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)θ=atan2(y,x).

What the original figure plots. The horizontal axis is the angle θ\thetaθ from −2π-2\pi−2π to 2π2\pi2π, and the vertical axis is tan⁡θ\tan\thetatanθ. The dashed vertical lines are the angles where tangent is undefined. The repeated branches show that tangent has period π\piπ; one branch is highlighted in red.

What this is trying to convey. When we calculate tan⁡θ=y/x\tan\theta=y/xtanθ=y/x, that ratio does not determine one unique angle. The same tangent value appears again after adding π\piπ, so an inverse tangent must pick one branch and cannot determine the quadrant by itself.

Powers and Roots of Complex Numbers¶

zn=(reiθ)n=rneiθnz^n = (r e^{\mathrm{i}\theta})^n = r^n e^{\mathrm{i}\theta n}zn=(reiθ)n=rneiθn
(12)

De Moivre’s theorem:

eiθn=(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)n=cos⁡(nθ)+isin⁡(nθ).e^{\mathrm{i}\theta n} = (\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^n = \cos(n\theta)+\mathrm{i}\sin(n\theta).eiθn=(cosθ+isinθ)n=cos(nθ)+isin(nθ).

Roots: solving wn=zw^n=zwn=z¶

For z=reiθz=re^{\mathrm{i}\theta}z=reiθ, solutions to wn=zw^n=zwn=z are

wk=r1/nei(θ+2πkn),k=0,1,…,n−1.w_k = r^{1/n} e^{\mathrm{i}(\frac{\theta+2\pi k}{n})},\qquad k=0,1,\dots,n-1.wk​=r1/nei(nθ+2πk​),k=0,1,…,n−1.
(14)

Roots are equally spaced around a circle radius r1/nr^{1/n}r1/n.

Trigonometric functions¶

Recall the Euler formula: ez=ex+iy=exeiy=ex(cos⁡y+isin⁡y)e^z = e^{x+\mathrm{i}y} = e^x e^{\mathrm{i}y } = e^x (\cos y+\mathrm{i}\sin y)ez=ex+iy=exeiy=ex(cosy+isiny)

We can write a pair of equations:

eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θe^{\mathrm{i}\theta} = \cos \theta + \mathrm{i}\sin \thetaeiθ=cosθ+isinθ
(15)
e−iθ=cos⁡θ−isin⁡θe^{- \mathrm{i}\theta} = \cos \theta - \mathrm{i}\sin \thetae−iθ=cosθ−isinθ
(16)

And solve them for sin⁡\sinsin and cos⁡\coscos:

sin⁡θ=eiθ−e−iθ2i\sin \theta = \frac{e^{\mathrm{i}\theta} - e^{- \mathrm{i}\theta}}{2 \mathrm{i}}sinθ=2ieiθ−e−iθ​
(17)
cos⁡θ=eiθ+e−iθ2\cos \theta = \frac{e^{\mathrm{i}\theta} + e^{- \mathrm{i}\theta}}{2}cosθ=2eiθ+e−iθ​
(18)

Hyperbolic functions¶

Trigonometric formulas can be generalized for complex numbers z as:

sin⁡z=eiz−e−iz2i\sin z = \frac{e^{\mathrm{i}z} - e^{- \mathrm{i}z}}{2 \mathrm{i}}sinz=2ieiz−e−iz​
(19)
cos⁡z=eiz+e−iz2\cos z = \frac{e^{\mathrm{i}z} + e^{- \mathrm{i}z}}{2}cosz=2eiz+e−iz​
(20)

Rewriting them for pure imaginary z=iyz = \mathrm{i}yz=iy gives:

sin⁡(iy)=e−y−ey2i=iey−e−y2=isinh⁡y\sin(\mathrm{i}y) =\frac{e^{-y}-e^y}{2\mathrm{i}} =\mathrm{i}\frac{e^y-e^{-y}}{2} =\mathrm{i}\sinh ysin(iy)=2ie−y−ey​=i2ey−e−y​=isinhy
(21)
cos⁡(iy)=e−y+ey2=cosh⁡y\cos(\mathrm{i}y) =\frac{e^{-y}+e^y}{2} =\cosh ycos(iy)=2e−y+ey​=coshy
(22)

These functions are called hyperbolic sine sinh⁡\sinhsinh and hyperbolic cosine cosh⁡\coshcosh. Their definitions for all z:

sinh⁡z=ez−e−z2\sinh z = \frac{e^{z} - e^{-z}}{2 }sinhz=2ez−e−z​
(23)
cosh⁡z=ez+e−z2\cosh z = \frac{e^{z} + e^{-z}}{2 }coshz=2ez+e−z​
(24)

Hyperbolic functions (continued)¶

sinh⁡z=ez−e−z2\sinh z = \frac{e^{z} - e^{-z}}{2 }sinhz=2ez−e−z​, cosh⁡z=ez+e−z2\cosh z = \frac{e^{z} + e^{-z}}{2 }coshz=2ez+e−z​

Note

Example Prove the identity: cosh⁡2z−sinh⁡2z=1\cosh^2 z - \sinh^2 z = 1cosh2z−sinh2z=1

What the original figure plots. It overlays three functions of a real variable xxx: sinh⁡x\sinh xsinhx as a solid red curve, cosh⁡x\cosh xcoshx as a dashed green curve, and tanh⁡x\tanh xtanhx as a dotted blue curve. They share the same axes so their different symmetry, growth, and limiting behavior can be compared directly.

What this is trying to convey. The exponential definitions produce three distinct qualitative shapes: sinh⁡x\sinh xsinhx is odd and unbounded, cosh⁡x\cosh xcoshx is even with a minimum of one, and tanh⁡x\tanh xtanhx is odd but bounded between -1 and 1.

Logarithms¶

  • Recall that for any z≠0z \neq 0z=0, if z=eω → ω=ln⁡zz = e^\omega \ \rightarrow \ \omega = \ln zz=eω → ω=lnz.

  • Using the law of exponents: z1z2=eω1eω2=eω1+ω2z_1 z_2 = e^{\omega_1} e^{\omega_2} = e^{\omega_1 + \omega_2}z1​z2​=eω1​eω2​=eω1​+ω2​

  • For the multivalued logarithm, log⁡(z1z2)=log⁡z1+log⁡z2\log(z_1z_2)=\log z_1+\log z_2log(z1​z2​)=logz1​+logz2​ is understood modulo 2πi2\pi\mathrm{i}2πi. A chosen principal branch does not obey the product rule globally.

  • Applying this idea to a polar form: ω=ln⁡z=ln⁡(reiθ)=ln⁡r+i(θ+2πk)\omega = \ln z = \ln (re^{\mathrm{i}\theta}) = \ln r+ \mathrm{i}(\theta + 2\pi k)ω=lnz=ln(reiθ)=lnr+i(θ+2πk)

  • On the conventional principal branch,

    Log⁡z=ln⁡r+iArg⁡z,Arg⁡z∈(−π,π].\operatorname{Log}z=\ln r+\mathrm{i}\operatorname{Arg}z, \qquad \operatorname{Arg}z\in(-\pi,\pi].Logz=lnr+iArgz,Argz∈(−π,π].
    (25)
Note

Example Compute ln⁡(−1)\ln(-1)ln(−1).

Complex Roots and Powers¶

  • Starting with ln⁡ab=bln⁡a\ln a ^b = b \ln alnab=blna,

  • We arrive at ab=ebln⁡aa^b = e^{b \ln a}ab=eblna

  • Because the complex logarithm is multivalued, the definition ab=eblog⁡aa^b=e^{b\log a}ab=ebloga generally produces a set of values. For special exponents, some or all of those values may coincide.

Applications in Physical Chemistry¶

Quantum Mechanics: complex wavefunctions¶

iℏ∂ψ∂t=H^ψ.i \hbar \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial t} = \hat{H} \psi.iℏ∂t∂ψ​=H^ψ.
(26)

A free particle solution: ψ(x,t)=Aei(kx−ωt)\psi(x,t) = A e^{i(kx - \omega t)}ψ(x,t)=Aei(kx−ωt)

What the original figure plots. It plots Re⁡ψ\operatorname{Re}\psiReψ and Im⁡ψ\operatorname{Im}\psiImψ as two sinusoidal functions of position xxx. They have the same amplitude and wavelength, but their peaks and zero crossings are shifted relative to one another.

What this is trying to convey. A single complex exponential contains two real sinusoidal components in quadrature. For ψ=Aeiϕ\psi=Ae^{\mathrm{i}\phi}ψ=Aeiϕ with ϕ=kx−ωt\phi=kx-\omega tϕ=kx−ωt, the real part is Acos⁡ϕA\cos\phiAcosϕ and the imaginary part is Asin⁡ϕA\sin\phiAsinϕ.

What the original figure plots. It sketches an arbitrary complex wavefunction ψ(x,0)\psi(x,0)ψ(x,0) by plotting two real-valued curves on the same axes: Re⁡ψ\operatorname{Re}\psiReψ in red and Im⁡ψ\operatorname{Im}\psiImψ in blue. The dashed lines labeled A--E mark selected positions where the two component values can be read and compared.

What this is trying to convey. A general complex wavefunction requires two real-valued component functions. Those components are amplitudes rather than probabilities; the measurable probability density is their squared combination ∣ψ∣2=(Re⁡ψ)2+(Im⁡ψ)2|\psi|^2=(\operatorname{Re}\psi)^2+(\operatorname{Im}\psi)^2∣ψ∣2=(Reψ)2+(Imψ)2.

The figures in this section are optional teaching candidates. They are kept at the end so they can be judged separately from the lecture itself.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Arc, Polygon

GOLD = "#cfb991"
DARK_GOLD = "#8e6f3e"
BLACK = "#000000"
GRAY = "#6f727b"

plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 120,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,

Cartesian and polar descriptions of the same number¶

This construction makes xxx, yyy, rrr, and θ\thetaθ visible at the same time, so conversion between the two notations becomes geometric rather than a list of formulas.

z = 3 + 2j
x, y = z.real, z.imag
r, theta = abs(z), np.angle(z)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 5.2))
ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, linewidth=1)
ax.axvline(0, color=GRAY, linewidth=1)
ax.plot([0, x], [0, y], color=DARK_GOLD, linewidth=3)
ax.scatter([x], [y], s=70, color=BLACK, zorder=4)
ax.plot([x, x], [0, y], "--", color=GRAY)
ax.plot([0, x], [y, y], "--", color=GRAY)
ax.add_patch(Arc((0, 0), 1.7, 1.7, theta1=0,
                 theta2=np.degrees(theta), color=GOLD, linewidth=3))
ax.text(x + 0.12, y + 0.08, r"$z=x+iy=re^{i\theta}$")
ax.text(x / 2 - 0.2, y / 2 + 0.2, rf"$r={r:.2f}$", color=DARK_GOLD)
ax.text(0.92, 0.18, rf"$\theta={np.degrees(theta):.1f}^\circ$")
ax.text(x / 2, -0.35, rf"$x={x:.0f}$", ha="center")
ax.text(x + 0.18, y / 2, rf"$y={y:.0f}$", va="center")
ax.set(xlim=(-0.7, 4.4), ylim=(-0.7, 3.4), aspect="equal",
       xlabel="real part", ylabel="imaginary part",
       title="One complex number, two coordinate systems")
plt.show()

Multiplication as scaling and rotation¶

The same multiplier acts on every point by one common scale factor and one common angle. Showing a small shape before and after the multiplication makes that global action easier to recognize.

w = 1.35 * np.exp(1j * np.deg2rad(38))
shape = np.array([0.5+0.4j, 2.3+0.4j, 2.3+1.6j, 0.5+1.6j, 0.5+0.4j])
mapped = w * shape

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.4), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, points, title, color in [
    (axes[0], shape, "Original points z", BLACK),
    (axes[1], mapped, "After multiplication: wz", DARK_GOLD),
]:
    ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, linewidth=1)
    ax.axvline(0, color=GRAY, linewidth=1)
    ax.plot(points.real, points.imag, "o-", color=color, linewidth=2)
    ax.plot([0, points[1].real], [0, points[1].imag], "--", color=GOLD)
    ax.set(aspect="equal", xlim=(-1.8, 3.2), ylim=(-0.5, 3.6),
           xlabel="Re", ylabel="Im", title=title)
fig.suptitle(rf"$w={abs(w):.2f}e^{{i{np.degrees(np.angle(w)):.0f}^\circ}}$: scale, then rotate")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Roots arranged as a regular polygon¶

All nnn roots have the same magnitude and equally spaced arguments. The plot turns the otherwise easy-to-miss 2πk/n2\pi k/n2πk/n term into a visible symmetry.

n = 5
target = 2 * np.exp(1j * np.deg2rad(70))
k = np.arange(n)
roots = abs(target)**(1/n) * np.exp(1j * (np.angle(target) + 2*np.pi*k) / n)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.3, 5.4))
ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, linewidth=1)
ax.axvline(0, color=GRAY, linewidth=1)
ax.add_patch(Polygon(np.c_[roots.real, roots.imag], closed=True,
                     fill=False, edgecolor=GOLD, linewidth=2))
ax.scatter(roots.real, roots.imag, s=90, color=DARK_GOLD, zorder=3)
for index, root in enumerate(roots):
    ax.plot([0, root.real], [0, root.imag], color=GRAY, alpha=0.55)
    ax.text(root.real * 1.13, root.imag * 1.13, rf"$k={index}$", ha="center")
ax.set(aspect="equal", xlim=(-1.7, 1.7), ylim=(-1.7, 1.7),
       xlabel="Re", ylabel="Im", title=f"The {n} distinct {n}th roots of z")
plt.show()

The principal-argument branch cut¶

Comparing the continuously increasing angle with the principal argument shows exactly where and why the value jumps at the negative real axis.

angle = np.linspace(-2*np.pi, 2*np.pi, 900)
principal = (angle + np.pi) % (2*np.pi) - np.pi

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.2, 4.2))
ax.plot(angle / np.pi, angle / np.pi, color=GRAY, linewidth=2,
        label="unwrapped angle")
ax.plot(angle / np.pi, principal / np.pi, color=DARK_GOLD, linewidth=2.5,
        label="principal Arg")
for cut in (-1, 1):
    ax.axvline(cut, color=BLACK, linestyle="--", alpha=0.65)
ax.set(xlabel=r"angle around the origin, $\theta/\pi$",
       ylabel=r"reported argument divided by $\pi$",
       yticks=[-2, -1, 0, 1, 2],
       title="Principal Arg wraps angles into one interval")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

ChatGPT-assisted extensions¶

For any of these assignments, students may use ChatGPT as a provisional collaborator, but the submission must include the important prompts, an independent mathematical check, at least one correction or limitation, and the student’s own conceptual explanation. ChatGPT output by itself is not evidence.

  1. Branch-cut detective. Give ChatGPT a set of complex logarithms, roots, and noninteger powers for points near the negative real axis. Determine whether it has silently used a principal value where all values were requested. Plot the arguments and branch cut, repair any missing values, and explain precisely which operations are multivalued.

  2. Build and audit a complex iteration. Ask ChatGPT to write a short Python experiment for zn+1=zn2+cz_{n+1}=z_n^2+czn+1​=zn2​+c or another simple complex recurrence. Test several initial points, visualize their paths in the complex plane, and use modulus and argument—not the picture alone—to explain why two paths behave differently. Identify one conclusion the finite computation cannot prove.

  3. Global phase versus relative phase. Ask ChatGPT to explain why multiplying a quantum state by one global phase does not change probabilities, while a relative phase can change interference. Construct a two-component numerical example, calculate the relevant probabilities in two bases, and critique any wording that confuses a complex amplitude with an observable probability.
